verdict.reasoning: Patient reports “really, really strong headache… started in the morning… I feel like dizzy. My vision is a little bit blue flourish… really painful,” and later confirms left-sided (“The left side only”) and vomiting (“I vomit twice… I still feel nausea”).
Doctor summarizes: “this morning… about four hours ago, you've developed a headache on the left side of the head… left side of the head, exactly,” matching onset this morning and ~4 hours duration.
Doctor asks, “Was it a sudden onset headache? Did it come on suddenly?” Patient answers, “Yeah, yeah, yeah… It came like kind of suddenly.”
Doctor asks for pain scale; patient: “let's say that that's 10 I have now maybe five. Well, six. … Six probably.”
Patient: “My vision is quite blurred… Like some zigzag lines…” and later “I cannot stand screens.”
Patient: “I vomit twice, actually… As soon as the headache started… and I still feel nausea. I'm about to vomit very soon, I think.”

Patient: “if I leave bed I start to feel like even worse if I move. So I just want to have my head like really not moving,” consistent with dizziness worse with movement and preferring to keep head still.

Doctor: “Have you noticed any weakness in your arms or legs?” Patient: “No… No.” And “when you're walking… or is your walk… funny?” Patient: “Not really.” Doctor summarizes: “you've got no neurological symptoms. You're walking fine.”
Patient: “the headache started like… four hours ago… I would say like maybe three hours ago [I took paracetamol] because I couldn't stand it.” Doctor: “you've taken paracetamol and it hasn't helped.”
Doctor: “Is there any chance you could be pregnant?” Patient: “I really doubt it.”
Patient: “I feel that this can be some kind of brain tumor or something… Or maybe a stroke… you hear so many stories… if I should go to A and E urgently.”
Patient: “Well, I had the kidney stone…” and doctor: “You've mentioned in the past you've had kidney stones.”
Doctor: “Do you take any regular medications?” Patient: “No.”
Doctor: “Are you allergic to any medications?” Patient: “Not that I'm aware. Yeah, not that I'm aware.” Doctor reiterates, “you're not allergic to any medications? Fine.”
Patient: “My mother has migraines… I’m very familiar with the disease because my mother has it.”
Patient: “And also, I have hypothyroidism in the family… She also has hypothyroidism.” Doctor repeats “Hypothyroidism.”
The transcript contains no vital signs or physical examination findings; only history is discussed. Therefore, stating that none are documented is accurate.

Doctor: “it sounds like what you're suffering from is what's known as a migraine… because it's on one side of the head… you've got blurry vision… with the nausea and vomiting… you've got no neurological symptoms. You're walking fine.” This matches the summarized assessment.

Patient self-describes: “Well, I'm a little bit hypochondriac… this can be some kind of brain tumor… Or maybe a stroke… if I should go to A and E urgently,” indicating health anxiety about serious intracranial pathology, which the clinician engages with.
Doctor: “I would recommend… take some medications, maybe something like ibuprofen… They can be ibuprofen with an anti sickness which you can get from the pharmacy.”
Doctor: “And also to drink a sugary carbonated drink, something like coke.”
Doctor: “Then we can go up the treatment ladder. You can get specific migraleve medication. And that's just something to try between now and when we see you.”

Doctor: “we can see you today at some point… we see you to do the assessment… However, if you do take these medications and… you feel much better… you can cancel it. You can give us a call and cancel it.” This implies a same-day in-person review for exam that may be cancelled if symptoms resolve.
Doctor: “Any further problems between now and your appointment, please do let us know.” This instructs contacting the clinic if further problems occur before the appointment.
